research_topic: Valkey/Redis coordination patterns for ADR 0004 (Valkey as Coordination Kernel)
transcript_summary: Deep research session investigating Valkey/Redis coordination patterns to validate and expand ADR 0004 (Valkey as Coordination Kernel). The session covered 8 topics: streams (O(1) insert, radix tree), consumer groups (at-least-once delivery, PEL, XCLAIM/XAUTOCLAIM), sorted sets for due-time wheel scheduling, TTL leases with SET NX EX and DELIFEQ, pub/sub vs streams tradeoffs, Valkey vs Redis comparison, Netflix Conductor and Temporal production patterns, and Lua scripting/Functions for atomicity. The goal was to validate the ADR's architectural decisions with primary sources and production evidence, and identify any gaps or risks in the coordination kernel design.

research_findings.title: Valkey Streams as Radix-Tree Append-Only Logs
research_findings.finding: Streams are implemented as radix trees providing O(1) insert with XADD and O(log N) seek + O(M) range read with XRANGE/XREADGROUP. Each entry gets a monotonic `<millisecondsTime>-<sequenceNumber>` ID that is clock-jump-safe. XADD supports inline trimming (MAXLEN, MINID). This validates ADR 0004's decision to use streams as the primary work-queue primitive — the performance characteristics align with coordination kernel requirements.

research_findings.title: Consumer Groups: At-Least-Once Delivery with PEL and Failure Recovery
research_findings.finding: XREADGROUP delivers each message to exactly one consumer in a group. The Pending Entries List (PEL) tracks unacknowledged messages per consumer. XACK removes from PEL after successful processing. For failure recovery, XAUTOCLAIM (Valkey 7.0+) scans PEL and claims messages idle past a threshold, replacing the manual XCLAIM+XPENDING loop pattern. This gives at-least-once delivery semantics. ADR 0004's reliance on consumer groups for work distribution is validated — but PEL monitoring is critical as it grows unbounded under backpressure.

research_findings.title: Sorted Sets as Due-Time Wheel with Atomic Lua Poll-and-Dequeue
research_findings.finding: Sorted sets are dual-ported (skip list + hash table) with O(log N) inserts and O(log N + M) range reads. The due-time wheel pattern uses score = Unix timestamp and ZRANGEBYSCORE to poll for due tasks. A Lua script can atomically poll and dequeue: ZRANGEBYSCORE to find due tasks, then ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to remove them. This validates ADR 0004's timing wheel design — but watch for score collisions at same millisecond (lexicographic fallback), lack of native retry/DLQ (must be layered), and no cron expression support.

research_findings.title: TTL Leases: SET NX EX Atomicity and DELIFEQ Simplification
research_findings.finding: SET key value NX EX seconds atomically creates a key only if it doesn't exist, with a TTL. The old SETNX+EXPIRE pattern is obsolete — SET NX EX is the correct approach. For safe release, a Lua script compares the stored value before deleting (GET + conditional DEL). Valkey 9.0 introduces DELIFEQ which eliminates the Lua script overhead for this pattern. Heartbeat renewal should run at 1/3 of TTL interval. ADR 0004's lease model using SET NX EX is validated — and the recommendation to target Valkey 9.0+ for DELIFEQ is supported.

research_findings.title: No Strong Consistency Across Failover: Coordination Primitives Lose State
research_findings.finding: Valkey is primarily async-replicated — failover can lose recent writes. This means all coordination primitives (leases, stream positions, scheduled tasks) can be lost on a failure. ADR 0004 correctly identifies this and designs around it with the PGlite rebuild protocol. The recovery mantra — 'anything you cannot reconstruct after a Valkey wipe does not belong only in Valkey' — is architecturally sound and consistent with Valkey's documented consistency model.

research_findings.title: Netflix Conductor: Production-Proven Stream/WQ Coordination
research_findings.finding: Netflix Conductor uses Redis (and now Valkey-compatible) as its primary coordination kernel for workflow/task metadata, task queues, and execution history. The storage layer is pluggable (Cassandra, MySQL, PostgreSQL alternatives), but Redis/Valkey is the default. Worker-task queue architecture mirrors ADR 0004: stateless workers poll for tasks, execute, update status. This validates the pattern — a production system used at Netflix scale runs on the same architectural model Tribunus proposes.

research_findings.title: Temporal: Comparison Point — Different Architecture for Different Needs
research_findings.finding: Temporal uses append-only event history in Cassandra/PostgreSQL as its durable core — NOT Redis. Redis is used as a complement for caching activity results and cross-workflow coordination locks. Temporal provides exactly-once guarantees via replay and supports Saga patterns natively. This is a different tradeoff from Conductor/Tribunus: Temporal trades Redis simplicity for stronger durability guarantees. The key insight for ADR 0004: Tribunus's PGlite + Valkey split mirrors Temporal's Cassandra + Redis split — one durable store for memory, one fast store for coordination.

research_findings.title: Valkey 9.0+: Hash Field Expiration and DELIFEQ Enable Simplification
research_findings.finding: Valkey 9.0 (October 2025) introduces hash field expiration (per-field TTL for HSET) and multiple databases in cluster mode — both directly relevant to ADR 0004. DELIFEQ simplifies safe lease release. SIMD optimizations (BITCOUNT/HLL 200% faster) and 1B+ req/s throughput are beyond current needs but future-proof. The 2026 roadmap includes Raft/lease-based consensus (exploratory), semantic caching, SSD tiering, and database consolidation. ADR 0004 should be updated to reference these features and consider targeting Valkey 9.0+ as a minimum.

research_findings.title: Valkey vs Redis: Licensing, Governance, and Diverging Feature Sets
research_findings.finding: Valkey (BSD 3-Clause, Linux Foundation) is the clear choice for open-source projects over Redis (AGPLv3 + RSALv2 + SSPLv1 tri-license). Valkey 8.0 delivers 1.2M req/s (3x Redis 7.2) with 70% latency reduction. Fully compatible with Redis 7.2 wire protocol. >1M container pulls/week as of early 2026. AWS and Google Cloud offer managed Valkey. The Linux Foundation governance with contributors from AWS, Google, Oracle, Ericsson, Alibaba, and Tencent provides long-term stability. ADR 0004's Valkey choice is validated — and the divergence from Redis means Tribunus should commit to Valkey-specific features (DELIFEQ, hash field expiration, cluster-mode multi-db) rather than maintaining Redis compatibility.

research_findings.title: Lua Script Runtime Limits and BUSY State Risk
research_findings.finding: Lua scripts execute atomically and block other commands during execution. The lua-time-limit defaults to 5000ms. Scripts exceeding this limit are killed (with potential data inconsistency) unless SCRIPT KILL is issued. Valkey 9.0 improved Lua scripting security but the fundamental risk remains: long-running scripts block the entire coordination kernel. ADR 0004 must ensure all Lua scripts are sub-millisecond for coordination operations (lease check-and-release, poll-and-dequeue) — heavier logic must be in the worker, not the Lua script.

research_findings.title: Stream PEL Growth Under High Backpressure
research_findings.finding: Valkey does not enforce a maximum PEL entry limit — the PEL can grow unbounded under sustained backpressure, causing memory pressure and slower XCLAIM scans. The mitigation is MAXLEN trimming on the stream and monitoring PEL size in production. ADR 0004 should document this risk and recommend operational monitoring for PEL size with automatic alerting.

research_findings.title: Pub/Sub vs Streams: Ephemeral vs Durable Communication
research_findings.finding: Valkey Pub/Sub provides fire-and-forget at-most-once delivery with sub-millisecond latency via push protocol. No persistence means messages are lost if a subscriber is offline. Streams provide at-least-once delivery, persistence, consumer groups, and replay capability. ADR 0004's rule — 'if the event matters after a restart, it is not pub/sub material' — is correct. The recommended combined pattern (streams for durable ingestion, pub/sub for instant push notifications) aligns with production best practices.

research_findings.title: Lua Scripting and Valkey Functions: Atomicity Guarantees
research_findings.finding: Lua (EVAL/EVALSHA) provides full atomic conditional logic but scripts are not persisted across restarts — clients must handle NOSCRIPT errors. Valkey Functions (7.0+) are first-class database artifacts that survive restarts and failovers, making them more production-grade for critical coordination logic. Key patterns for ADR 0004: atomic lock release (GET+conditional DEL), atomic lock renewal (GET+conditional PEXPIRE), atomic poll-and-dequeue (ZRANGEBYSCORE+ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), and atomic counter with TTL. MULTI/EXEC with WATCH is simpler but lacks Lua's conditional power.

research_findings.title: Redlock Complexity Not Warranted for Single-Region Coordination
research_findings.finding: Redlock requires 5 independent Valkey primaries, sequential SET NX on each, and majority quorum. Martin Kleppmann's critique identifies fundamental issues: assumed bounded clock drift, lack of fencing tokens (monotonic counter for resource servers), and GC pause vulnerability. For ADR 0004's single-region Tribunus use case, single-instance locking with unique tokens is sufficient — Redlock's complexity is unwarranted. The recommendation is to use single-instance SET NX EX with Lua check-and-release, and only consider Redlock if multi-datacenter operation becomes necessary.

research_findings.title: Combined Primitive Architecture: Streams + Sorted Sets + TTL + Lua
research_findings.finding: Production coordination kernels combine multiple Valkey primitives: streams for work queues (durable, ordered, consumer groups), sorted sets for scheduling (due-time wheel, priority queues), TTL keys for leases (leader election, heartbeats, work claims), and Lua scripts for atomic compound operations (poll-and-dequeue, check-and-release). ADR 0004's architecture uses all four primitives correctly. The key insight: all Valkey coordination primitives lose state on async-replicated failover — the PGlite rebuild protocol is not optional but fundamental to the architecture. Single-instance locking with fencing tokens is sufficient for Tribunus.

research_findings.title: Valkey 2026 Roadmap: Raft Consensus, SSD Tiering, Hybrid Search
research_findings.finding: Valkey's 2026 roadmap includes stronger consistency via Raft/lease-based consensus (exploratory), semantic caching plus hybrid search (vector + full-text) for RAG, compression plus SSD tiering, and 'database consolidation' — reducing the number of specialized stores. If Raft consensus is implemented, it could eventually provide the strong consistency that ADR 0004 currently compensates for with the PGlite rebuild protocol. This doesn't change the ADR today but is worth tracking for future simplification.

implementation_specs.title: Valkey Coordination Kernel Implementation
implementation_specs.description: Implementation specifications for the Valkey coordination kernel as defined in ADR 0004. Covers stream-based work queues, sorted set scheduling, TTL leases, Lua scripting for atomic operations, Valkey Functions for persisted coordination logic, PEL monitoring, rebuild protocol, and operational configuration.
acceptance_criteria: Stream consumer groups deliver each message to exactly one worker
XAUTOCLAIM recovers stuck messages after configurable idle timeout
Sorted set due-time wheel dispatches tasks within 1-second accuracy
TTL leases with SET NX EX provide deadlock-free mutual exclusion
Lua scripts execute all compound coordination operations atomically
DELIFEQ (Valkey 9.0+) used for safe lease release where available
PEL monitoring alerts on pending message accumulation beyond threshold
Rebuild protocol restores Valkey state from PGlite within 1 second
AOF persistence configured with appendfsync everysec for local desktop
Pub/Sub used only for ephemeral signals not requiring durability

implementation_patterns.name: Stream Consumer Group Work Queue
implementation_patterns.description: XGROUP CREATE for group creation, XREADGROUP for consumer read, XACK for acknowledgment, XAUTOCLAIM for failure recovery. Each stream represents a work queue (missions, packet submissions, gates, PRs).
implementation_patterns.code_example:
XGROUP CREATE missions:review review-workers $
XREADGROUP GROUP review-workers worker-1 COUNT 1 STREAMS missions:review >
XAUTOCLAIM missions:review review-workers worker-2 30000 0-
XACK missions:review review-workers 1728394859293-0

implementation_patterns.name: Sorted Set Due-Time Wheel
implementation_patterns.description: ZADD with Unix timestamp score for scheduled tasks. Lua script for atomic poll-and-dequeue: ZRANGEBYSCORE to find due tasks, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to remove, return results.
implementation_patterns.code_example:
ZADD schedule:missions 1728394859 mission:abc-123
local tasks = server.call('ZRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], '-inf', ARGV[1])
if #tasks > 0 then
  server.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], '-inf', ARGV[1])
end
return tasks

implementation_patterns.name: TTL Lease with SET NX EX
implementation_patterns.description: Atomic lease acquisition with SET NX EX, Lua check-and-release for safe release, heartbeat renewal at 1/3 TTL interval. Fencing tokens for distributed safety.
implementation_patterns.code_example:
SET lease:task-123 worker-uuid-456 NX EX 30
if server.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return server.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end

implementation_patterns.name: Valkey Functions for Persisted Coordination Logic
implementation_patterns.description: Prefer Valkey Functions (7.0+) over raw EVAL for critical atomic operations that must survive restarts. FUNCTION LOAD to define, FCALL to execute.
implementation_patterns.code_example:
FUNCTION LOAD '#!lua name=lease
local v = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
if v == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DELIFEQ', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
else return 0 end'
FCALL lease 1 lease:task-123 worker-uuid-456
